💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent.
  • Industry observers note that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves.
  • Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

Industry observers note that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”.

In a recent development, these people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

Sources indicate that if you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”.

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”.

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

According to recent reports, in many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person remarked.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another stated, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person said, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”.

In a recent development, it’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person mentioned.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”.

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly notable for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”.

According to recent reports, naming rustout won’t solve the matter, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

Recent findings suggest that from my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others noted, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”.

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

It has been revealed that they may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

In a recent development, for organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

Recent findings suggest that that is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

Industry News: The Egg McMuffin Order You Can Only Find In Canada

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mcDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu.
  • According to recent reports, the Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin.
  • Sources indicate that to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mcDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu. Alongside familiar faves, you'll find items Americans can't order, the most envy-inducing among them arguably being the Egg BLT McMuffin. Once you hear what's in it, don't be surprised if you catch yourself planning a trip to our northern neighbor.

According to recent reports, the Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin. A second version uses nearly identical ingredients but swaps the whole leaves for shredded lettuce. You can only get this variation at McDonald's restaurants located inside Walmart stores — part of a decades-old partnership that once placed roughly 1,000 outposts in the retail chain. McDonald's later closed hundreds of them as drive-thrus became the main source of sales, though Walmart continues to host many locations in Canada.

Sources indicate that to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative. Your best bet is to start with a Bacon, Egg & Cheese McMuffin, which already ticks off half the ingredients. Ask for a touch of mayo, which gets you close to the sauce of the Canadian original. Since lettuce and tomatoes are lunchtime items, your odds improve near the end of breakfast hours when stores are prepping the lunch menu — you'll likely have to order them at the counter or window.

Recent findings suggest that the Egg BLT might have already convinced you to add McDonald's to your itinerary next time you're in Canada, but it's not the only breakfast item worth the detour. One that caught our eye was the Mighty McGriddles. While the U.S. offers the Bacon, Egg & Cheese and Sausage, Egg & Cheese varieties separately, the Canadian version puts both to shame by stacking a double helping of hickory-smoked bacon, a sausage patty, egg, and cheese between two maple-flavored griddle cakes — a gloriously overstuffed creation that lives up to its name. The Mighty McMuffin follows the same logic, coming loaded with both meats for anyone who can never decide between the two.

Industry observers note that another familiar face on Canadian McDonald's breakfast menus is the bagel, though while America only offers plain, Canada also serves sesame and everything varieties. You can even order one toasted with butter or Philadelphia cream cheese — widely known as the best store-bought brand — as if you're at a proper bagel shop.

It has been revealed that canada's McDonald's restaurants aren't afraid to put a twist on U.S. staples, and they also introduce fresh items altogether. You won't find chicken anywhere on the standard U.S. breakfast menu, which makes the Chicken McGriddles feel like a curveball up north. The simple yet delicious sandwich pairs a breaded chicken patty with two sweet, maple-flavored griddle cakes for some serious sweet-and-savory fusion.

#92140. 14 French Desserts You Should Try Once In Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2418 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

14 French Desserts You Should Try Once In Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • French cuisine is largely known for its decadent textures, flavors, and presentations, and this includes a long list of regional desserts.
  • If you aren't already familiar with French desserts, it doesn't matter if you are fluent in the language or not; the names of the country's culinary creations don't always alert you to what they actually are.
  • The tart Tatin may have a fancy name, but don't let that fool you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French cuisine is largely known for its decadent textures, flavors, and presentations, and this includes a long list of regional desserts. We all know about croissants, and, yes, when infused with the right sweet elements, they definitely count as a dessert, but that's just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to French desserts. In fact, there is a seemingly never-ending list of eye-catching sweet treats that hail from the country. The ones found below, though, are so mouthwateringly delicious that everyone should try them at least once in their lives.

If you aren't already familiar with French desserts, it doesn't matter if you are fluent in the language or not; the names of the country's culinary creations don't always alert you to what they actually are. With this in mind, if you're interested in sampling a few — why wouldn't you be? — but aren't sure where to start, we can help point you in the right direction. So, get your fork and spoon ready, because once you learn about the collection of French desserts below, you'll be dying to get your hands on them.

The tart Tatin may have a fancy name, but don't let that fool you. It is actually akin to an apple pie, just flipped upside down — and there's nothing extravagant about that. The French version of the dessert also has humble origins. As the story goes, in the late 1800s, Caroline (of Caroline and Stephanie Tatin's Inn, located south of Paris) forgot to put a crust on the bottom of her apple pie. Due to being exceptionally busy, she decided to put it on top instead and see what would happen. When she took it out of the oven and flipped it over, she saw that her misstep led to a happy result: The apples were beautifully caramelized. When she served it to the inn's guests, it was an immediate success, and the tarte Tatin was officially born.

Industry observers note that creating a tart Tatin is fairly accessible to novice home cooks. It only calls for five ingredients: apples, flour, butter, eggs, and sugar. The trickiest part is arranging the slices of fruit in a decorative way on the bottom of the pan. Actually, despite her massive culinary repertoire, Ina Garten admits it is the recipe she makes most because it is not only delicious, but easy to create, as well. If it's good enough for Garten to come back time and time again, you'd better believe it's a French dessert everyone should give a go at least once.

Crème brûlée is one of the most easily recognizable and widely popular French desserts in the United States, but, interestingly enough, its origins are somewhat disputed. France, England, and Spain all claim to be the birthplace of the dessert. Regardless, since its invention, wherever that happened to be, there's no doubt it has fully integrated itself into traditional French cuisine, and if you've never had the joy of eating one before, you are truly missing out.

In its most basic format, crème brûlée is made with just four ingredients: egg yolks, sugar, heavy cream, and vanilla bean. While simple, the elements come together to form a creamy, custardy delight. Then, the top is scorched to form a layer of burnt sugar that's to die for. Topping it with a couple of fresh berries is also customary, but either way, it is simplicity at its finest. In fact, this is one case where the sum is much greater than its parts. In addition to the sweet, rich flavor of the custard itself, part of the fun of eating one is using a spoon to crack the burnt layer on top. It not only adds a caramelized taste but contributes textural variation, and that is always a plus. Whether you decide to try your hand at making crème brûlée yourself or choose to seek it out from a restaurant, it's a French dessert that's worth your attention.

Éclairs have been around since the 1860s, and today, they are one of the more popular French desserts found in the United States. For good reason, too; they are tasty enough to go down in a flash. Speaking of which, the word directly translates to lightning.

Sources indicate that name and popularity aside, éclairs are made with choux pastry, which is similar to doughnut pastry, but devoid of baking soda, baking powder, and yeast, and relies on steam to rise. As a result, after being formed into long cylindrical pieces, the dough cooks up to be exceptionally light and airy. That's just the start of the legendary éclair, though. They are also filled with pastry cream or custard and then topped with either fondant or ganache icing — both of which are harder styles of icing, so you can still feel free to enjoy éclairs with your hands.

Arguably, the most popular flavor of éclair is chocolate, but thanks to the versatility of the choux pastry shell, they are welcoming to a world of other flavors as well. Everything from caramel to pistachio to Nutella to strawberry to matcha with chocolate and beyond can be found enhancing the delightful little pastry.

Industry observers note that french yogurt cake, or gâteaux au yaourt in the native language, is another easy yet extremely satisfying dessert that deserves some time in the spotlight. In France, it is a popular recipe for kids to learn, likely because of the simple recipe, which calls for three eggs, one part oil, one part yogurt, two parts sugar, three parts flour, and leavening. Even so, when it comes out of the oven, you have a drool-worthy, slightly tangy cake that is moister than pound cake (if you can fathom that) while still presenting a delicate crumb.

In a recent development, since French yogurt cake is not a common restaurant offering, if you want to give it a taste, you'll likely have to make one yourself. Or, at the very least, enlist a friend to do it — um, mom? Thankfully, though, it is one of the more straightforward must-try French desserts out there, so it should be attainable for even the most novice home cooks. The simplicity of the French yogurt cake also makes it prime for a plethora of flavor infusions. So, if you want to add citrus, or brandy, or fruit to the mix, go right ahead.

According to recent reports, crêpes are a delicately thin pancake-like creation that's ready and waiting for a world of flavor and ingredient infusions. Still, a Crêpes Suzette is quite possibly the most delicious and famous version of them all. It consists of classic crêpes in a sauce made of sugar, orange juice, and an orange liqueur, like Gran Marnier. The entire thing is also smothered in brandy and set on fire, which leads to a caramelized, citrusy, sweet flambé sauce that will draw just about anyone in. Heck, even watching a chef prepare one catches the eye, and that's why it's often done in full view when ordered in a restaurant.

Interestingly enough, crêpes Suzette is another iconic French dessert that was first created by accident — and this particular story is not disputed. In 1895, Henri Carpentier, a 14-year-old assistant waiter at the Maitre at Monte Carlo's Cafe Paris, was preparing dessert for the Prince of Wales (who'd later become King Edward VII of England). While doing so, he accidentally caught the cordials he was working with on fire, and instead of becoming flustered and starting over from scratch, he tasted the sauce and realized he'd come up with something extraordinary.

Don't let the flambé scare you too much if you want to try creating one at home; it truly does lead to exceptional flavor. However, you can still make a tasty rendition sans the potential fire hazard; it just won't be quite as authentic.

In a recent development, first and foremost, Mont Blanc is known for being the highest mountain in the Alps. However, for those in the know, it is also a delectable French sweet treat with Alpine-inspired appeal. In fact, when created, the Mont Blanc dessert resembles a snow-capped mountain peak, so the name is more than fitting. The exact origins of it is uncertain, but a reigning theory is that it was developed in Paris, France, in the 19th century. During that era, chestnuts started to grow in popularity in the region, and people began incorporating them into sweet dishes, instead of the customary savory ones.

The main components of a Mont Blanc dessert are as follows: It starts with a crisp meringue base, which is topped with thin strands of chestnut purée, and then finished off with a pile of whipped cream. Traditionally, a vermicelli tip is used to pipe the chestnut puree, but other shapes are also common. Either way, though, the yummy chestnut puree is the star of the show, offering a nutty, rich flavor that offsets the creamy whipped cream and meringue in a delightful way.

According to recent reports, hailing from the Basque region in southwest France, the Gâteau Basque became widely popular in the 19th century. Its growth in the culinary scene is largely attributed to a particular baker, Marianne Hirigoyen, who first sold them in local markets before opening a brick-and-mortar bakery. Since then, the gâteau Basque's acceptance into French culinary tradition has been more than cemented. Actually, fast-forward to today, and there's now a museum and a two-day festival in October dedicated to the dessert. If that doesn't tell you exactly why it is a must-try French recipe, we don't know what would.

According to recent reports, whether you call them canelé, cannelé de Bordeaux, or canelé Bordelais, these yummy little French pastries are time-consuming to make — the dough needs to rest for up to 24 hours before baking. Even so, their delectable mix of textures and delicious buttery, custard-y flavors are worth the effort used to make them and then some.

Industry observers note that small and cylindrical with fluted edges, the center of canelés are made with flour, milk, sugar, butter, vanilla bean, eggs, salt, and rum. Once mixed with care, the dough rests for an extended time before baking in copper molds. After they're cooked, a delicious coating of edible beeswax and butter fills the molds and is also poured over the top before baking again. When that's done, you're left with delicious bite-sized (well, almost) custard-filled cakes featuring a caramelized crust on the exterior. Considering miniature copper fluted molds are not a customary tool in most homes, canelés aren't the first dessert we recommend trying to make at home. However, if you ever see them in a French bakery or restaurant, you'd be a fool not to give them a try.

Opera cake is one of the coffee desserts that are always worth ordering, and guess what? It's also a French dessert everyone should try at least once. That is, of course, if you know what's good for you — and in this case, we truly hope you do.

Created by Cyrique Gavillon, the opera cake is just as much a thing of beauty as it is a delectable flavor wonderland. A rectangular-shaped cake at heart, it is made with alternating layers of coffee syrup-soaked almond cake, buttercream, and ganache, and then topped with a rich dark chocolate icing. Once completed, it not only looks stunning, but provides your palate with a mix of nutty, chocolatey, creamy, rich, coffee flavors that are hard to beat. Yes, it sounds a whole lot like tiramisu when the elements are taken at face value, but it is a delightful dessert all its own when it comes to how the ingredients come together. Plus, it's French, not Italian. Just saying.

According to recent reports, while simple to make, the Île flottante presents itself as an elegant dish, and as such, is a mainstay in French cuisine. In fact, while it's mentioned French people prefer to purchase dessert from a local bakery, it is one recipe many natives still have in their repertoire. It just so happened to be Julia Child's favorite old-school dessert, as well. Since she is credited with bringing French cuisine to the United States and helping it grow in popularity, following her lead regarding the greatest culinary hits of the country just makes sense.

According to recent reports, similar to éclairs, which we've already discussed, profiteroles are made with hollowed-out choux pastry, filled with custard or cream, and topped with icing. What sets them apart is their shape. Instead of being long and cylindrical, profiteroles are formed into small bite-sized balls. As a result, they are the perfect sweet treat for bringing to a gathering or munching on if you simply want a few bites. However, once you get a taste of their scrumptious textures and flavors, trying to eat just one will be quite a complicated task.

It has been revealed that again, like éclairs, the most common icing flavor for profiteroles is chocolate. Still, they come in a myriad of other flavors, as well, so they have what it takes to pique the interest of many. For example, if chocolate is too one-dimensional for you — we are judging you — you can also make chocolate hazelnut profiteroles, vanilla ones, or just about any other flavor you can dream up.

According to recent reports, last but certainly not least on our list of French desserts you need to try is clafoutis. The name may sound posh, but it's actually another sweet treat that's incredibly easy to make, so you don't have to be an established French baker to create one at home. Plus, it may be a dessert, but it is also acceptable to eat it for breakfast. Okay, now we are really listening.

Recent findings suggest that clafoutis consists of fruit smothered with a thick custard made from sugar, flour, milk, and eggs. The texture is akin to flan, but undeniably has all the French flair a Francophile could want. Most traditionally, cherries create the meaty fruit of clafoutis, but other berries and fruits, like raspberries, are also commonly used to pull off the recipe. While not necessarily a dessert, if you want to go in a savory direction, fruit can also be substituted for prosciutto, cheese, and tomatoes, so think of it like a choose-your-own-adventure type dish. No matter how you build it, though, clafoutis is one French creation that deserves more recognition, at least in the States.

It has been revealed that A grilled cheese is already plenty hearty, but the common tip of using cured meats to increase its satisfying flavor — like in this tasty maple bacon variation — may interfere with your filling's texture if you prefer a smooth, gooey filling. Duck fat is the perfect way around this because it adds meatiness without changing any other ingredients, enriching the bread with umami with just a single smear.

Recent findings suggest that duck fat is one of the most prized cooking fats in the culinary world because it has a higher smoke point than butter (around 375 degrees Fahrenheit) and a beautifully silky texture rich in subtle, meaty flavors. Just like spreading it on burger buns, using duck fat on grilled cheese can give you crispier bread because you can cook it at a higher temperature. When left at room temperature, it has a consistency similar to softened butter, making it easy to spread or drop in a pan, depending on your preference. Its unique composition of fats and subtle meaty flavor mean you'll notice its richness even in small amounts. Though it has a touch of gaminess, it's quite subtle and serves to elevate creamy and aged cheeses alike with an added layer of complexity.

Using duck fat on grilled cheese is pretty easy, but there are a few tricks that can really maximize your results. Blending it with another fat, using it for some added seasoning, and picking the right pan can all give you the perfect sandwich.

Recent findings suggest that mixing a fat with a high smoke point with one that burns more easily is a simple way to combine the best of both worlds. The richness of butter is irreplaceable, but you can incorporate some of duck fat's higher-heat cooking properties by swirling the two together before spreading the mix on your bread. Similarly, you can also bring your duck fat to a low, gentle simmer and add herbs and aromatics to flavor it beforehand. Whether you do this when rendering the fat yourself or just for a few minutes before adding your sandwich, a bit of sage can lend tremendous depth, while a smashed clove of garlic can mimic the rich flavor of toum.

Industry observers note that while a nonstick pan is great for butter since it doesn't retain as much heat, you might want to go in the opposite direction for duck fat. A heavy cast iron or stainless steel skillet helps prevent the surface temperature from dropping when you add the sandwich, maintaining that lovely heat that makes duck fat work so well. Plus, animal fats are great for cast iron's seasoning, helping you maintain your pan's coating while you cook!

In a recent development, the actual difference between a hamburger and a steakburger comes down to the quality of meat used in the grind, but the difference between a homemade steakburger and one from a steakhouse is all about a lighter texture. Melissa Clark, author of "The Big Book of Dinner: Recipes and Rules (and How to Break Them)," tells us that achieving that characteristic is quite easy if you use ground cracker crumbs.

Industry observers note that "Any kind of cracker or breadcrumbs will make a burger lighter," Clark says. "Ritz and saltines work really well. They are very airy, which helps lighten the ground meat." Beef is rather dense, even if you avoid overworking it into a firm, puck-like consistency that's more similar to sausage than a tender patty. But a quarter cup of ground crackers per pound of meat can make a world of difference.

When meat cooks, it contracts and releases juice and fat. Crackers, however, absorb them rather than allowing them to seep out of the patty, preventing it from shriveling up too much. Since steakhouse burgers typically use thick patties, this also keeps them nice and moist. Whereas a thin sliver of well-crusted beef may be just what you want in a smashburger, retaining moisture is a vital component to keeping your steakhouse burgers not only light, but also at their peak flavor.

It has been revealed that using plain, unsalted crackers can still keep your steakhouse burgers light, but it would be a missed opportunity for better flavor. While you also don't want to use something starch-free, like a nut- or seed-based variety, Melissa Clark is a substantial believer in picking a tasty brand and smashing them up properly.

"Using crackers can add great flavor – Ritz, with their butteriness, are especially lovely," Clark explains. Flavorful but unobtrusive, Ritz crackers are the perfect addition to any savory dish because just about everything can benefit from their toasty richness. But if you want to get a bit experimental, you can also just as easily use Cheez-Its or anything seasoned. This is an easy way to avoid coming up with a specialty spice blend since you'll be adding enough to thoroughly flavor your meat.

According to recent reports, clark is also a proponent of using whatever method you can to grind the crackers into a fine powder. "Grind the crackers in a food processor, blender or tuck them in a plastic bag and crush them under a rolling pin," she added. Large chunks can make some bites unexpectedly soggy and, if using a seasoned cracker, a little too flavorful. Plus, if some parts of your blend don't have a starch, they may end up expressing their juices too much, leaving some bites juicy and light and others dense and dry.

Breaking: Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

Recent findings suggest that according to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, mentioned, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”.

Homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who right now serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”.

According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”.

The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.

Recent findings suggest that this article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

Among the most iconic Middle Eastern dishes, hummus blends chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice, and optional seasonings to delicious effect. It's a dish that can be assembled at home, but many tasty store-bought versions are available, too. If your grocery store hummus happens to taste a little flat, though, reach for toum. Just a spoonful of this condiment will make a version that's 10 times better.

It has been revealed that hailing from Lebanon, toum is an emulsion made by blending a generous dose of garlic with oil, lemon juice, and sometimes water. Smooth and airy in texture yet with an underlying bite, it lends hummus a dose of garlicky goodness and acidity, readily transforming a bland flavor into a complex one. Plus, the condiment packs in extra fat, helping to improve the perceived creaminess of disappointingly dry hummus. Since toum is a homogeneous paste, it's easy to incorporate, and its flavor can be less aggressive than raw garlic, too.

You won't need much toum to make an impact. Start by mixing in just under a teaspoon per standard 8-ounce container, then work in gradual increments from there. For ease, grab a jar of toum online, or peruse the same grocery aisles where you bought the hummus. You could also easily prep your own toum in bulk — the condiment typically keeps for up to a month in the fridge.

In a recent development, A toum-inflected hummus makes a great dip, scooped up with za'atar-dusted pita chips, pretzels, veggie chips, or whatever other crisp your heart desires. Note that there are many other ways to use hummus in everyday cooking, though — especially when it's mixed with toum.

For example, consider topping the condiment with spiced ground beef or lamb, a popular Middle Eastern combination. Flavor the minced meat with earthy spices and fiery chilies, and the garlicky hummus makes for a mouthwatering flavor combo, turning the store-bought dip into an extra-hearty meal.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, make the chickpea-based dip less of a centerpiece and use it as a sandwich spread instead — it would pair delectably with crunchy vegetables like cucumbers and onions, as well as greens like spinach. Served on whole-grain bread, the dip makes for a delicious vegetarian meal.

Recent findings suggest that looking for an extra creative twist? You could even use the toum hummus to make your next batch of tuna salad — the garlicky flavor will pair terrifically with the tinned fish. When you're craving Middle Eastern flavors but don't feel like cooking, keep the toum-hummus pairing in mind.

The fat enhances the bread's crispiness, all while retaining a moist interior. As a sole filling, the spread turns the dish luxuriously decadent — but complemented with a few slices of cheese, it's a grilled cheese rendition to remember.

There are many international grilled cheese styles to explore; cheddar cheese spread fits into a wide range of renditions. Combined with a store-bought loaf of sourdough and sliced cheddar, the spread makes a mouth-watering classic. However, you can consider layering in other ingredients, too — thereby making a cheddar grilled cheese with a twist.

For a sweet touch with less sugar, you could also use fresh fruits to upgrade any grilled cheese; the spread would go great with apples, for example, as apples and cheddar are a match made in sandwich heaven. And you could also consider leaning into the spice, smearing on spicy brown mustard or hot pepper jelly for a light dose of heat.

Sources indicate that consider trying out other ingredient add-ins, too. Caramelized onions will lend a grilled cheese a subtle nutty sweetness, while bacon bits bring a savory touch. Cheddar cheese spreads allow the many different flavors to come together, letting you easily craft a sandwich to your tastes.

#92125. 22 Recipes To Make With Thanksgiving Leftovers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2531 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

22 Recipes To Make With Thanksgiving Leftovers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey, ham, mashed potatoes, casseroles, pumpkin, cranberries, stuffing ...
  • Especially when you're hosting a crowd (which is possible to do stress-free with these tips from Guy Fieri), those leftovers can be abundant.
  • If you're looking for newly introduced ideas or creative ways to use up what's left in the fridge, we've got a plethora of recipes to try that'll help you make the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey, ham, mashed potatoes, casseroles, pumpkin, cranberries, stuffing ... the annual fall-flavored feast that we know and love is always a crowd-pleasing holiday meal to look forward to. And one of the best things about Thanksgiving isn't just the meal itself; it's all of the delicious leftovers that inevitably follow.

Especially when you're hosting a crowd (which is possible to do stress-free with these tips from Guy Fieri), those leftovers can be abundant. But the beauty is that there's so much more you can do with your Thanksgiving leftovers than just reheat and re-eat. From soups, sandwiches, and snacks that repurpose your ingredients to completely fresh dishes that transform the original elements of the meal, you can take those leftovers in so many directions.

If you're looking for newly introduced ideas or creative ways to use up what's left in the fridge, we've got a plethora of recipes to try that'll help you make the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. (Pro tip: Just don't forget the 2-2-2 rule with your leftovers to ensure food safety.).

It has been revealed that whether you enjoyed some mac & cheese on Thanksgiving Day or not, this recipe is a whole latest twist on the classic that infuses the beloved dish with holiday flavor. It's honestly a little shocking how many leftover ingredients manage to make their way into this one recipe, but when you think about it ... how could it not taste good?

Sources indicate that this Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese incorporates three different types of cheese — fontina, cheddar, and mascarpone — to make the cheese sauce. Then come the Thanksgiving leftovers that get folded into the dish: shredded turkey meat, sweet potatoes, peas, and pasta. After it's baked, the whole thing is topped off with some cranberry sauce to bring the Thanksgiving flavors home.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese.

It has been revealed that now, this is a fun one — it's Thanksgiving dinner in burger form! Not only can you use that leftover stuffing, but this recipe also calls for turkey meat, gravy, and cranberry sauce, so this one wins for maximizing whatever's taking up space in the fridge. And it's incredibly tasty, too.

The "burger" is a combination of stuffing, turkey, eggs, and milk in patty form. The patty is then griddled in some butter and topped off with cranberry sauce, gravy, and goat cheese to create a burger that'll leave you stuffed in the best way.

Recipe: Leftover Thanksgiving Stuffing Burger.

Okay, a turkey cheesesteak might seem a little contradictory, but this one's worth entertaining when it comes to making the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. You won't just knock out the leftover turkey, but also any leftover gravy with this Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak.

The cheesesteak starts with sautéed sweet onions, and then the turkey (dark meat works great if you have it), gravy, and cornichons are added to the mix before two types of cheese (provolone and American cheese) are melted on top. Everything is stuffed into toasty hoagie rolls to make a saucy, messy, tasty Thanksgiving cheesesteak.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak.

Why not whip up the ultimate comfort meal to enjoy the weekend after Thanksgiving? Once the holiday winds down, you can use your leftover turkey (and any extra pumpkin puree you might have lying around) in this Pumpkin and Turkey Chili recipe. This fall take on a classic slow cooker chili recipe incorporates pumpkin puree into the stew along with a blend of warm spices like cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg.

To sub in your already-cooked turkey, just skip the initial step where you'd brown the ground turkey, and instead add some cubed or shredded turkey once your chili is simmering.

Recipe: Pumpkin and Turkey Chili.

Making croquettes is a fun and delicious way to use up that leftover turkey. Croquettes actually originated in France as a way to use up leftover meats and vegetables, so they're the perfect way to repurpose those Thanksgiving leftovers.

The cheesy croquettes are made by sautéeing mushrooms, onions, and garlic and combining the mixture with cooked turkey, parsley, and mozzarella cheese. They're then shaped into balls, dipped into egg and breadcrumbs, and lightly fried until golden brown and crispy.

Recipe: Crispy Turkey and Cheese Croquettes.

According to recent reports, shepherd's pie is a great follow-up recipe to Thanksgiving if you need a way to reuse copious amounts of mashed potatoes, because that iconic mashed potato topping makes shepherd's pie what it is. This particular recipe is made with ground lamb and vegetables like corn, peas, and carrots as the base of the pie, but you could easily sub in your leftover turkey as well if you want to knock out two leftovers in one go.

It has been revealed that either way, this Simple Shepherd's Pie is even easier to make since the mashed potatoes are already done. All you need to do is assemble, bake, and enjoy ... or if you're feeling ambitious, you can try one of these 15 secret ingredients to make your Shepherd's Pie the best it can be.

Bought too many potatoes on your Thanksgiving grocery run? This casserole will come in handy for those extra ingredients. The simple, easy-to-make dish combines potatoes, onions, bacon, and thyme with cream, chicken stock, and cheese. Everything gets baked until it's melty and delicious, making a perfect side dish to pair with any leftover meat from the holiday.

This recipe uses blue cheese, which complements the bacon, but you can feel free to use any cheese you like (cheddar, mozzarella, or even Gruyère would all work great).

Recipe: Potato Bacon Cheese Bake.

This comforting soup brings together many ingredients that were most likely on your Thanksgiving shopping list, including carrots, apples, potatoes, and pecans. It's the perfect meal to throw together that'll make use of all of those extra groceries that you're not sure what to do with. Carrots and apples may not be your first thoughts as the base of a soup, but trust us, this comforting soup recipe is a (somewhat unexpected) winner.

All you need to do is cook your vegetables down with plenty of flavorful herbs and spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, and fresh thyme. Add your stock, blend until smooth, and finish off with the cream for a nutty and rich yet soothing soup that you can work your way through all week.

Recipe: Nutty Carrot and Apple Soup.

For all those who may have purchased some fresh pumpkins for your Thanksgiving pie but didn't get around to using all of it, we've got just the recipe. As a bonus, it'll use up those extra potatoes, too!

Put a fall spin on a classic potato gratin by slicing your pumpkin into pieces or rounds the same size as your potatoes. The cream mixture, which is made up of heavy cream, garlic, thyme, rosemary, and salt, gets layered with your pumpkin and potatoes; then everything is covered with grated Swiss cheese and baked longer than you may think until the whole dish is bubbly, browned, and cheesy.

Recipe: Herbed Pumpkin Potato Gratin.

According to recent reports, whether you've got some extra sweet potatoes lying around from a casserole side dish or a sweet potato pie, this Sweet Potato Tarte Tatin is a delicious way to use them up. And with a little puff pastry, this dish looks impressive but doesn't take long to make a classic tarte tatin.

The trick is making the caramel element; once you've gotten that down, the rest is smooth sailing. Your homemade caramel will come together with sliced sweet potatoes and a puff pastry covering to produce an irresistible starchy take on the tarte tatin.

Recipe: Sweet Potato Tarte Tatin.

Similar to the tarte tatin, you can use a store-bought dough (this time, paper-thin Greek phyllo pastry) to keep this dessert simple. Baklava is typically made with nuts, but this recipe replaces that crunchy ingredient with a smooth pumpkin puree — along with spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove — for a tasty fall twist on this decadent, flaky treat.

Industry observers note that baklava involves making a simple syrup of sorts, and then it's all about layering (and this hack for assembling can make your baklava process even quicker). In the end, you'll have an extremely crispy, sweet-yet-spiced dessert born from leftover pumpkin puree.

Recent findings suggest that if there's one thing you may not have thought to do with your leftover pumpkin and cranberries, it might be homemade liqueur. It might seem a little extreme, but it's not as complicated as it sounds, and you will be rewarded with an ingredient that'll help level up your baking and cocktails for many weeks to come.

In short, the process just involves cooking down your chosen ingredient with sugar, then adding a high-proof liquor like vodka, and then straining it and letting it sit. That's it!

Recipe: Cranberry Liqueur and Pumpkin Liqueur.

In a recent development, if you didn't quite make as much apple pie filling as you planned, don't worry — this one's for you. It's basically a shortcut apple pie filling that you can throw on some ice cream, douse in whipped cream, or simply enjoy on its own.

This Sweet Spiced Baked Apples recipe is one of the easiest ways to make use of all of those leftover apples. Any apples will do: Honeycrisp, Fuji, Pink Lady, you name it. All you need to do is bake them with an undeniably delicious mixture of brown sugar, walnuts, butter, and spices. It's so simple, and so satisfying.

Recipe: Sweet Spiced Baked Apples.

Sources indicate that sticking with those leftover apples, this recipe will make a fantastic breakfast or brunch in the days following Thanksgiving. The Americanized origins of Dutch baby pancakes are a bit complicated, but long story short, this creation is essentially a giant, skillet-baked pancake. And it's a great go-to dish to capitalize on your extra apples, because you most likely have everything else you need stocked in your kitchen.

Recent findings suggest that this Dutch baby recipe uses a batter made of flour, milk, eggs, honey, vanilla extract, salt, and melted butter. Next, pour the batter over thinly sliced apples that have been tossed in brown sugar and cinnamon. Everything is then baked together to perfection until your leftover apples turn into puffy, golden goodness.

Sources indicate that this is a unique and flavorful way to use any extra pumpkins you have from the holiday. The bonus? The presentation is impressive, so if you find yourself continuing to host through the weekend, this is another great meal to provide for your guests that will help you repurpose some of your Thanksgiving ingredients.

With everything from coconut milk and ground pork to ginger, soy sauce, and water chestnuts, this rice dish includes a lot of really interesting ingredients that may not seem like they belong together, but they all unite to build a warm, aromatic meal. Just trust the process, serve it up inside a pumpkin, and watch your guests marvel.

Recipe: Stuffed Pumpkin With Aromatic Rice.

Although this recipe includes a lot of similar ingredients as the above (rice, pumpkin, nuts), the elements come together in a totally different way to create a totally different dish: a warmly spiced, sweet rice pudding that'll taste just like your Thanksgiving pumpkin pie.

The dessert is made with Arborio rice, almond milk, maple syrup, pumpkin puree, vanilla, and spices — everything gets simmered together until it thickens into a pudding, then chilled and served with glazed pecans for extra crunch.

Recipe: Vegan Pumpkin Pecan Rice Pudding.

It has been revealed that leftovers truly shine when you use them to build a great sandwich. Meet this Sweet and Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich, which can be made with your leftover Thanksgiving turkey and ham. In addition to the sliced duo of meat, this sandwich features Gruyère cheese, mayo, and raspberry jam (although you can obviously sub in some cranberry sauce if you so please), all stacked between slices of brioche bread.

What makes this Monte Cristo extra delicious is the French toast treatment that it gets: Once assembled, the entire sandwich is dipped in a mixture of egg, half-and-half, and nutmeg and lightly fried in butter until golden brown. Oh, it's then topped off with some powdered sugar for good measure.

Recipe: Sweet And Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich.

Here's another fun breakfast recipe to keep things interesting over the holiday weekend! This take on a Croque Madame (a classic French sandwich typically made with ham, cheese, and Mornay sauce and topped with a sunny-side-up egg) creates a "waffled" version of the sandwich by employing a waffle iron as the cooking tool.

Where do the leftovers come in? The waffle "batter" is made with your leftover Thanksgiving stuffing, which you'll then combine with milk and eggs. This concoction is then topped with slices of ham and grated cheddar cheese, and finished off with a fried or poached egg. Post-Thanksgiving brunch is served.

Sources indicate that if you've still got some sweet potatoes left from your holiday shopping, this is another great recipe to make use of them — and it couldn't be simpler. This Sweet Potato and Sausage Hash makes a great breakfast or brunch, and can be topped with some eggs or eaten on its own. And all it takes is six ingredients to get there.

The dish starts with some onions and garlic sautéed in butter. These are then combined with cooked Italian sausage and cubed sweet potatoes. Everything is roasted together in a cast-iron skillet, showing how you can make this recipe with minimal effort and maximum tastiness.

Recipe: Sweet Potato and Sausage Hash.

It has been revealed that there are never enough ways to use up those extra potatoes! This time, your floury potatoes like Yukon Golds or Russets take the lead with an herby potato galette. This particular recipe is a crustless galette, so there's no dough necessary, and you only need a handful of ingredients to make it.

To make the galette, shred the potatoes, add them to a hot skillet with lots of olive oil and sage, then press them down to help form a natural crust. Cook the potatoes for another 10 minutes as butter is added to the pan, then flip the whole thing and cook it on the other side. The result is a crispy potato pancake that's golden on the outside, soft on the inside, and delicious all the way around.

Recipe: Potato Galettes With Sage.

Recent findings suggest that it's the ultimate Thanksgiving grilled cheese, so you don't want to pass this one up. You can make use of several leftover ingredients for this sandwich, both savory and sweet, such as extra apples and leftover ham.

Industry observers note that apple butter is spread across two slices of sourdough bread, and then layered with Brie, diced ham, and diced apples before the sandwich is toasted in butter. This simply isn't your average grilled cheese sandwich; you also get bonus points if you can pair it with some butternut squash soup.

Recipe: Sweet and Savory Brie and Apple Butter Grilled Cheese.
